`hello.world`                                   -> "", "", false
`hello|world`                                   -> `hello`, `world`, true
`a|b|c`                                         -> `a`, `b|c`, true
`hello\|world`                                  -> "", "", false   (escaped pipe)
`hello.#`                                       -> "", "", false
`hello.#[a|1="asdf\"|1324"]#\|that`             -> "", "", false
`hello.#[a|1="asdf\"|1324"]#|that.more|yikes`   -> `hello.#[a|1="asdf\"|1324"]#`, `that.more|yikes`, true
`a.#[]#\|b`                                     -> "", "", false
`a.#|b`                                         -> "", "", false   (the char after ".#" is skipped)

`a.#\|b`                                        -> `a.#\`, `b`, true (the "\" after ".#" is skipped unexamined)

`a.#[x]|y`                                      -> `a.#[x]`, `y`, true
`a.#(b=="x|y")|z`                               -> `a.#(b=="x|y")`, `z`, true
`a.#(b(c)|d)|e`                                 -> `a.#(b(c)|d)`, `e`, true
`a.#[b(c|d]|e`                                  -> `a.#[b(c|d]`, `e`, true
`a.#(b="q\"|")#|c`                              -> `a.#(b="q\"|")#`, `c`, true
`.|x`                                           -> `.`, `x`, true
`a.|b`                                          -> `a.`, `b`, true
`a|`                                            -> `a`, "", true

# Functional specification: `func squash(json string) string`

## 1. Component overview

`squash` is an internal helper of the `gjson` package (`github.com/tidwall/gjson`),
a library that extracts values from JSON text without fully decoding it. Given a
string whose first character opens a JSON value (an array, an object, a
parenthesised group used by the path syntax, or a string literal), `squash`
returns the prefix of the input that contains exactly that one value, ignoring
whatever follows it. The library uses it to cut the raw text of nested
arrays/objects out of a larger document (e.g. when listing the members of an
array, building `Result.Raw`, or splitting modifier arguments such as
`@pretty:{"sortKeys":true}`).

The function does not validate JSON; it only tracks bracket nesting and string
literals.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. **Bracketed values.** If the first character is anything other than `"`,
   it is treated as the opener: it is skipped without being examined and the
   nesting depth starts at 1. Normally it is `[`, `{` or `(`, but callers also
   pass text whose first character is an ordinary byte (for a multipath such as
   `{a,b}|c`, the library calls `squash("a,b}|c")`, which returns `a,b}`); such
   a first character is treated exactly like an opener. Scanning the following
   characters:
   - any of `[`, `{`, `(` increases the depth by one;
   - any of `]`, `}`, `)` decreases it by one. The kinds are **not** matched
     against each other: `[` may be closed by `}` or `)`.
   - when the depth returns to 0, return the input up to and including that
     closing character.
2. **String literals are opaque.** A `"` outside a string starts a string
   literal. Everything up to its closing quote is skipped, so brackets inside
   strings are ignored. A quote is a closing quote only if it is preceded by an
   **even** number (including zero) of consecutive backslashes inside the
   literal; a quote preceded by an odd number of backslashes is escaped and
   does not end the string. Backslashes have no meaning outside string
   literals.
3. **String input.** If the first character is `"`, the input is a string
   literal. Return everything up to and including its closing quote (same
   escaping rule as above).
4. **Unterminated containers.** If a bracketed value never returns to depth 0
   (including the case where the input ends inside a string literal), return
   the whole input unchanged.
5. All other characters (digits, letters, `,`, `:`, whitespace, ...) are copied
   through untouched and have no effect on the scan.
6. The result is always a prefix (a substring starting at index 0) of the input.
   The function is pure and safe for concurrent use.

## 3. Input specification

- `json`: a non-empty Go string (arbitrary bytes, usually UTF-8). Its first
  byte is usually `[`, `{`, `(` or `"`, but may be any byte (rule 1).
- When the first byte is `"`, the string literal is always terminated in the
  input (an unterminated leading string literal is never passed).

## 4. Output specification

- A `string`: the prefix of `json` holding the first value, as described above.
- Multi-byte UTF-8 characters never affect the scan (all structural characters
  are ASCII).

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `[]` | `[]` |
| `{}` | `{}` |
| `()` | `()` |
| `""` | `""` |
| `{"a":[1,{"b":2}]},3` | `{"a":[1,{"b":2}]}` |
| `{"a":"]"}tail` | `{"a":"]"}` |
| `[("]")]x` | `[("]")]` |
| `(a(b)c) d` | `(a(b)c)` |
| `[}` | `[}` |
| `[[[]]]]]` | `[[[]]]` |
| `[1]   [2]` | `[1]` |
| `[1,2` | `[1,2` (never closed) |
| `["unterminated` | `["unterminated` |
| `"a\"b"x` | `"a\"b"` (escaped quote does not end the string) |
| `"a\\"b` | `"a\\"` (two backslashes: the quote closes the string) |
| `"\\\""tail` | `"\\\""` |
| `["\\"]x` | `["\\"]` |
| `{"a":"\"}"}rest` | `{"a":"\"}"}` |
| `"]"` | `"]"` |
| `a,b}|c` | `a,b}` (first character counts as the opener) |
| `x.#(a|b)}|c` | `x.#(a|b)}` |
| `a]` | `a]` |
| `ab` | `ab` (never closed) |

# Functional specification: `func tostr(json string) (raw string, str string)`

## 1. Component overview

`tostr` is an internal helper of the `gjson` package (`github.com/tidwall/gjson`),
which extracts values from JSON text without fully decoding it. It is called when
the parser reaches a JSON string literal: `json` is the remainder of a document,
starting at the opening `"`. `tostr` returns the raw text of the literal (as it
appears in the document) and its decoded value. `Parse` and the array/object
member listing (`Result.Array`, `Result.Map`, `Result.Value`) use it to fill in
`Result.Raw` and `Result.Str` for string values.

## 2. Functional requirements

Let the *closing quote* be the first `"` after the opening one that is preceded
by an **even** number (including zero) of consecutive backslashes. (A quote
preceded by an odd number of backslashes is escaped and belongs to the string.)

1. **No backslash before the closing quote.** If a closing quote is found and
   there is no `\` between the opening and the closing quote:
   - `raw` = the input up to and including the closing quote;
   - `str` = the characters between the two quotes, copied **verbatim** (no
     decoding; control characters such as a literal tab are kept).
2. **No backslash and no closing quote.** `raw` = the whole input and `str` =
   the whole input without its first character.
3. **Backslash present.** If a `\` occurs before the closing quote (or before
   the end of the input when there is no closing quote):
   - Let `end` be the index of the closing quote, or `len(json)` when there is
     none.
   - `str` = `unescape(json[1:end])`, i.e. the content between the opening quote
     and `end`, decoded exactly as the `unescape` function in the context does
     (decoding stops early at a raw control character, an unknown escape, or a
     truncated `\u` escape).
   - `raw` = `json[:end+1]` (through the closing quote) **if** there is at least
     one more character after the closing quote; otherwise (the closing quote is
     the very last character of the input, or there is no closing quote)
     `raw` = `json[:end]`. In other words, in the escaped case a closing quote
     that ends the input is *not* included in `raw`.
4. Text after the closing quote is ignored. The function is pure and safe for
   concurrent use; it never panics for inputs that meet section 3.

## 3. Input specification

- `json`: a Go string of length >= 1 whose first byte is `"`. The rest is
  arbitrary bytes (normally JSON string content, possibly with `\uXXXX`
  escapes, raw UTF-8, and trailing document text such as `,`, `]`, `}`).

## 4. Output specification

- `raw`: always a prefix of `json` (starting with the opening quote).
- `str`: the decoded string value as described above (valid or invalid UTF-8
  is passed through unchanged in the verbatim case; `\u` escapes are encoded as
  UTF-8, lone surrogates become U+FFFD as done by `unescape`).

Inputs and outputs below are shown as raw text; `<TAB>` is a literal tab byte.

| `json` | `raw` | `str` |
|---|---|---|
| `"hello"` | `"hello"` | `hello` |
| `"hello",1` | `"hello"` | `hello` |
| `""` | `""` | (empty) |
| `"",` | `""` | (empty) |
| `"abc` | `"abc` | `abc` |
| `"a<TAB>b"x` | `"a<TAB>b"` | `a<TAB>b` |
| `"中文",` | `"中文"` | `中文` |
| `"a\"b",` | `"a\"b"` | `a"b` |

| `"\\"x` | `"\\"` | `\` |

# Functional specification: `func unescape(json string) string`

## 1. Component overview

`unescape` is an internal helper of the `gjson` package (`github.com/tidwall/gjson`),
which extracts values from JSON text. When a JSON string literal contains
backslash escape sequences, the library passes the literal's body (the text
between the opening and the closing quote, quotes excluded) to `unescape` to get
the decoded Go string that ends up in `Result.Str` (and in object keys). It must
be lenient: malformed input never causes a panic; decoding simply stops.

## 2. Functional requirements

The input is processed left to right, appending to the output:

1. **Ordinary bytes.** Every byte `>= 0x20` (space) that is not a backslash is
   copied unchanged. This includes `"`, `/`, DEL (0x7F) and every byte of
   multi-byte UTF-8 sequences (raw UTF-8 passes through untouched, valid or
   not).
2. **Raw control bytes stop decoding.** On a byte `< 0x20` (e.g. a literal
   newline, tab or NUL), return the output produced so far; the rest is
   dropped.
3. **Simple escapes.** A backslash followed by one of these characters appends:
   `\\` -> `\`, `\/` -> `/`, `\"` -> `"`, `\b` -> 0x08, `\f` -> 0x0C,
   `\n` -> 0x0A, `\r` -> 0x0D, `\t` -> 0x09.
4. **Unknown or truncated escapes stop decoding.** A backslash that is the last
   byte, or that is followed by any other character (e.g. `\x`, `\q`, `\'`),
   ends decoding: return the output so far (the backslash and everything after
   it are dropped).
5. **`\u` escapes.** `\u` must be followed by at least 4 more bytes; if fewer
   than 4 bytes remain after the `u`, decoding stops (return the output so
   far). Otherwise those 4 bytes are read as a hexadecimal code unit
   (upper- or lower-case digits). If they are not 4 valid hex digits, the code
   unit is 0 (U+0000). Then:
   - If the code unit is a UTF-16 surrogate (0xD800–0xDFFF) **and** the next
     6 bytes exist and start with `\u`, those 6 bytes are consumed as a second
     code unit (again 0 if not valid hex), and the pair is combined as a UTF-16
     surrogate pair. If the two do not form a valid high+low pair (e.g. the
     first is a low surrogate, or the second is not a low surrogate), the
     result is a single U+FFFD and **both** escapes are still consumed.
   - A surrogate that is not followed by at least 6 bytes starting with `\u`
     becomes U+FFFD on its own; nothing after it is consumed and the following
     text is processed normally (e.g. `\ud83dabc` and `\ud83dA`).
   - The resulting code point is appended encoded as UTF-8 (U+0000 is a
     single 0x00 byte).
6. Returns the output as a Go `string`. Pure, no side effects, safe for
   concurrent use.

## 3. Input specification

- `json`: any Go string (possibly empty, arbitrary bytes). Usually the body of a
  JSON string literal, without the surrounding quotes.

## 4. Output specification

- The decoded `string`. Its length never exceeds what the decoded escapes
  produce; for an input without backslashes or control bytes the output equals
  the input.

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

Inputs are shown as raw text (`<NUL>` is a 0x00 byte, `<LF>` a 0x0A byte).

| input | output |
|---|---|
| (empty) | (empty) |
| `plain text` | `plain text` |
| `\\<NUL>` | `\` (the NUL stops decoding) |
| `\/\b\f` | `/`, 0x08, 0x0C |
| `\"quoted\"` | `"quoted"` |
| `tab\there` | `tab`, 0x09, `here` |
| `été` | `été` |
| `中中` | `中中` |
| `😀` | `😀` (U+1F600) |
| `𝄞` | `𝄞` (U+1D11E) |
| `\ud83d` | U+FFFD |
| `\ud83dabc` | U+FFFD then `abc` |
| `\ude00\ud83d` | U+FFFD (one character; both escapes consumed) |
| `\ud83dA` | U+FFFD then `A` (fewer than 6 bytes follow, so nothing extra is consumed) |
| `\ud83d\uzzzz` | U+FFFD |
| `\ud83d\u12` | U+FFFD (then `\u12` is truncated -> stop) |
| `end\ud83d\` | `end` then U+FFFD |
| `\u0000x` | 0x00 then `x` |
| `\uzzzzx` | 0x00 then `x` (invalid hex reads as 0) |
| `\u12`, `\u123` | (empty) |
| `ab\` | `ab` |
| `ab\x` | `ab` |
| `a<LF>b` | `a` |
| `a`, 0x7F, `b` | unchanged (0x7F is not a control byte here) |
| `\\\\` (4 backslashes) | `\\` |

- Must run in time linear in the input length.

# Functional specification: `func oomm(n, b *big.Int, maxmag int) (float64, int)`

## 1. Component overview

`oomm` ("order of magnitude, with a maximum") is an unexported helper of the
`humanize` package (`github.com/dustin/go-humanize`), in `big.go`. It works on
arbitrary-precision integers (`math/big`). Given a non-negative number `n` and
a base `b`, it finds how many times `n` can be scaled down by `b` (the
magnitude, optionally capped at `maxmag`) and returns the scaled-down value
as a `float64` together with that magnitude. `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` use it
with base 1000 or 1024 and a cap equal to the number of unit names, e.g. to
turn `15347691069326346944512` bytes into `"15 ZB"` / `"13 ZiB"`, and
`16093220510709943573688614912` into `"16093 YB"` (the cap stops the scaling
at the largest unit).

## 2. Functional requirements

Let `N` be the value of `n` at the start of the call and `B` the value of `b`.

1. **Magnitude.** The returned `mag` is the number of whole scaling steps
   performed, where one step replaces the current value `x` by `floor(x / B)`.
   Steps are performed while the current value is `>= B`.
   - If `maxmag >= 1`, scaling stops as soon as `mag` reaches `maxmag`, even
     if the current value is still `>= B`.
   - If `maxmag <= 0` there is no cap: scaling continues until the current
     value is below `B`. (Note: `maxmag == 0` behaves like "no cap", not
     like "zero steps".)
   - If `N < B`, no step is performed and `mag` is `0`.
2. **Value.** Let `q` be the value after the last step, i.e. `floor(N / B^mag)`,
   and let `r` be the remainder of the last step, i.e.
   `floor(N / B^(mag-1)) mod B` (and `r = 0` when `mag == 0`). The returned
   float is exactly the `float64` expression
   `float64(q) + float64(r)/float64(B)`, computed in that order with ordinary
   `float64` arithmetic. Only the remainder of the **last** step contributes
   to the fractional part; lower-order digits are discarded.
3. **Argument state.** `n` may be overwritten by the function (callers pass a
   scratch copy); its value after the call is unspecified. `b` must not be
   modified.
4. The function has no other side effects.

Examples (`(value, mag)`):

| `N` | `B` | `maxmag` | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `5` | `10` | `-1` | `(5, 0)` |
| `999` | `1000` | `8` | `(999, 0)` |
| `1500` | `1000` | `8` | `(1.5, 1)` |
| `12345` | `10` | `-1` | `(1.2, 4)` |
| `12345` | `10` | `0` | `(1.2, 4)` |
| `12345` | `10` | `2` | `(123.4, 2)` |
| `123456789` | `1000` | `1` | `(123456.789, 1)` |
| `5242880` | `1024` | `1` | `(5120, 1)` |
| `5242880` | `1024` | `8` | `(5, 2)` |
| `1024` | `1000` | `8` | `(1.024, 1)` |

## 3. Input specification

- `n`: non-nil `*big.Int`, value `>= 0`, of any size (up to thousands of
  decimal digits).
- `b`: non-nil `*big.Int`, value `>= 2` and small enough to fit in an
  `int64`.
- `maxmag`: any `int`; values `<= 0` mean "no cap".
- The inputs are always such that the final `q` fits in an `int64`
  (automatically true without a cap, since then `q < B`).

## 4. Output specification

- First result: `float64(q) + float64(r)/float64(B)` as defined above.
- Second result: `mag`, the number of steps performed (`0 <= mag`, and
  `mag <= maxmag` when `maxmag >= 1`).

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- `N == 0` or any `N < B`: returns `(float64(N), 0)`.
- `N == B`: one step, `q = 1`, `r = 0`, returns `(1, 1)`.
- With a cap, `q` may be much larger than `B` (e.g. `(123456.789, 1)` above).
- The result must be identical bit-for-bit to the expression in rule 2;
  in particular, do not include lower-order digits in the fraction, and do
  not compute the value as `N / B^mag` in floating point.
- The function never panics for inputs in the contract.

# Functional specification: `func ParseBigBytes(s string) (*big.Int, error)`

## 1. Component overview

`ParseBigBytes` is part of the `humanize` package (`github.com/dustin/go-humanize`).
It is the arbitrary-precision inverse of `BigBytes` / `BigIBytes`: it parses
a human-readable size such as `"42 MB"`, `"16.5 ZiB"` or `"1,005.03 MB"` into
an exact number of bytes as a `*big.Int` (from `math/big`). Both SI units
(powers of 1000) and IEC units (powers of 1024) are accepted, up to
yottabytes, and the result is never limited to 64 bits.

## 2. Functional requirements

The input is read as a **numeric prefix** followed by a **unit**.

1. **Numeric prefix.** The numeric prefix is the longest leading run of
   characters that are decimal digits, `.` or `,`. It ends at the first
   character that is none of these (a space, a letter, `-`, `+`, …). Commas
   in it are thousands separators and are ignored wherever they appear
   (`"1,005.03"` means `1005.03`, `"1,,2"` means `12`).
2. **Number.** After removing the commas, the prefix must be a decimal
   number made of digits with at most one `.` and at least one digit, e.g.
   `"42"`, `"42.5"`, `"5."`, `".5"`, `"007"`. Its value is taken **exactly**
   (as a rational number, with no floating-point rounding, however many
   digits it has). If it is empty or malformed (`""`, `"."`, `"1.2.3"`),
   return `nil` and a non-nil error.
3. **Unit.** The rest of the string, with leading and trailing white space
   removed and converted to lower case, must be one of:

   | unit (any case) | multiplier |
   |---|---|
   | `""` (no unit), `"b"` | 1 |
   | `"k"`, `"kb"` / `"ki"`, `"kib"` | 1000 / 1024 |
   | `"m"`, `"mb"` / `"mi"`, `"mib"` | 1000^2 / 1024^2 |
   | `"g"`, `"gb"` / `"gi"`, `"gib"` | 1000^3 / 1024^3 |
   | `"t"`, `"tb"` / `"ti"`, `"tib"` | 1000^4 / 1024^4 |
   | `"p"`, `"pb"` / `"pi"`, `"pib"` | 1000^5 / 1024^5 |
   | `"e"`, `"eb"` / `"ei"`, `"eib"` | 1000^6 / 1024^6 |
   | `"z"`, `"zb"` / `"zi"`, `"zib"` | 1000^7 / 1024^7 |
   | `"y"`, `"yb"` / `"yi"`, `"yib"` | 1000^8 / 1024^8 |

   (These are the entries of `bigBytesSizeTable` in the context.) Any other
   unit text is an error: return `nil` and an error whose message is
   `"unhandled size name: "` followed by the trimmed, lower-cased unit text
   (e.g. `"84 JB"` gives `unhandled size name: jb`).
4. **Result.** Multiply the exact number by the unit multiplier and return
   the largest integer not greater than the product (fractional bytes are
   dropped), as a newly allocated `*big.Int`, with a nil error. There is no
   upper limit.
5. **Error precedence.** The number is checked first: when both the number
   and the unit are invalid (e.g. `"1.2.3 JB"`, `"JB"`, `" 42 JB"`), the
   number error is returned (not `unhandled size name: ...`).
6. The function does not modify any package-level value (in particular the
   multiplier values must stay unchanged) and is safe for concurrent use.

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `"42"` | `42` |
| `"42MB"`, `"42mb"`, `"42 MB"`, `"42 M"`, `"42m"` | `42000000` |
| `"42MiB"`, `"42mib"`, `"42MIB"`, `"42 Mi"`, `"42 MI"` | `44040192` |
| `"42.5MB"`, `"42.5 M"` | `42500000` |
| `"42.5MiB"`, `"42.5 Mi"` | `44564480` |
| `"1,005.03 MB"` | `1005030000` |
| `"12.5 EB"`, `"12.5 E"` | `12500000000000000000` |
| `"12.5 EiB"` | `14411518807585587200` |
| `"16 EiB"` | `18446744073709551616` |
| `"15.99 EiB"` | `18435214858663483146` |
| `"16 ZB"`, `"16 Z"` | `16000000000000000000000` |
| `"16 ZiB"`, `"16 Zi"` | `18889465931478580854784` |
| `"16.5 ZiB"` | `19479761741837286506496` |
| `"16 YiB"` | `19342813113834066795298816` |
| `"16.5 YiB"`, `"16.5 Yi"` | `19947276023641381382651904` |
| `"0.9"`, `".5"` | `0` |
| `"1.9999999"` | `1` |
| `"3 \tk"` | `3000` |

prefix), `"-5"`, `"."`, `"1.2.3"`, `"1e3"` (unit `"e3"`), `"1 bytes"`.

## 3. Input specification

- `s`: any string. Inputs are ASCII. White space between the number and the
  unit, and after the unit, is allowed. The number may have many digits
  (hundreds or more) in its integer or fractional part.

## 4. Output specification

- On success: a non-nil `*big.Int` holding the byte count (always `>= 0`),
  and `nil`.
- On failure: `nil` and a non-nil `error`.

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- Leading white space or a sign before the number makes the numeric prefix
  empty, which is an error.
- Exponent notation is not supported (`"1e3"` is an error).
- Results beyond 64 bits are exact (`"16 EiB"` is `2^64`, not an error).
- Long fractional parts are exact: `"0.000000000000000000001 YB"` is `1000`.
- The function never panics.

## 1. Component overview

`ParseBytes` is part of the `humanize` package (`github.com/dustin/go-humanize`).
It is the inverse of `Bytes` / `IBytes`: it parses a human-readable size such
as `"42 MB"`, `"42MiB"` or `"1,005.03 MB"` into a number of bytes. Both SI
units (powers of 1000: kB, MB, …) and IEC units (powers of 1024: KiB, MiB, …)
are accepted, up to exabytes.

## 2. Functional requirements

The input is read as a **numeric prefix** followed by a **unit**.

1. **Numeric prefix.** The numeric prefix is the longest leading run of
   characters that are decimal digits, `.` or `,`. It ends at the first
   character that is none of these (for example a space, a letter, `-`,
   `+`). Commas inside it are thousands separators and are ignored wherever
   they appear (`"1,005.03"` means `1005.03`, `"1,0.5k"` means `10.5k`).
2. **Number.** After removing the commas, the prefix must be a valid decimal
   number for `strconv.ParseFloat(…, 64)`: digits with at most one `.`, e.g.
   `"42"`, `"42.5"`, `"5."`, `".5"`, `"007"`. It is converted to the nearest
   `float64`. If it is empty or invalid (e.g. `""`, `"."`, `"1.2.3"`), return
   `0` and the error produced by `strconv.ParseFloat`.
3. **Unit.** The rest of the string, after removing leading and trailing
   white space and converting to lower case, must be one of these unit names
   (case-insensitive in the input):

   | unit (any case) | multiplier |
   |---|---|
   | `""` (no unit), `"b"` | 1 |
   | `"k"`, `"kb"` | 1000 |
   | `"ki"`, `"kib"` | 1024 |
   | `"m"`, `"mb"` | 1000^2 |
   | `"mi"`, `"mib"` | 1024^2 |
   | `"g"`, `"gb"` | 1000^3 |
   | `"gi"`, `"gib"` | 1024^3 |
   | `"t"`, `"tb"` | 1000^4 |
   | `"ti"`, `"tib"` | 1024^4 |
   | `"p"`, `"pb"` | 1000^5 |
   | `"pi"`, `"pib"` | 1024^5 |
   | `"e"`, `"eb"` | 1000^6 |
   | `"ei"`, `"eib"` | 1024^6 |

   error: return `0` and an error whose message is
   `"unhandled size name: "` followed by the trimmed, lower-cased unit text
   (e.g. `"84 JB"` gives `unhandled size name: jb`).

# Functional specification: `func Commaf(v float64) string`

## 1. Component overview

`Commaf` is part of the `humanize` package (`github.com/dustin/go-humanize`),
which turns machine values into human-friendly text. It renders a `float64`
in plain decimal notation (never scientific notation) and inserts a comma
between every group of three digits of the **integer part** (English
thousands separators). The fractional part, if any, is kept exactly and is
not grouped. `CommafWithDigits(f, decimals)` in the same file builds on it by
cutting the result to a number of decimal places.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. **Digits.** The digits written are those of the shortest decimal string
   that converts back to exactly the same `float64` value, written in
   fixed-point form without an exponent. This is exactly the digit string of
   `strconv.FormatFloat(x, 'f', -1, 64)`, where `x` is `-v` when `v < 0` and
   `v` itself otherwise (negative zero is not `< 0`, so it is formatted as
   is, see rule 4).
   Consequently:
   - integral values have no decimal point: `100` gives `"100"`, not
     `"100.0"`;
   - very large values are padded with zeros instead of an exponent:
     `1e21` gives `"1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000"`;
   - very small values are written out in full: `1e-7` gives `"0.0000001"`.
2. **Grouping.** The integer part (everything before the decimal point) is
   split into groups of three digits counted from the right, separated by
   `,`. The leftmost group has 1 to 3 digits. Integer parts of 1 to 3
   digits contain no comma. Internal zeros are kept: `10001000` gives
   `"10,001,000"`.
3. **Fraction.** If the value has a fractional part, it follows the
   grouped integer part as `.` plus its digits, unchanged and without any
   separators: `834142.32` gives `"834,142.32"`, `100000.25` gives
   `"100,000.25"`.
4. **Sign.** A value strictly less than zero is written as `-` followed by
   the formatting of `-v`: `-123456789` gives `"-123,456,789"`, `-100.11`
   gives `"-100.11"`. Negative zero compares equal to zero, so it is not
   "below zero"; it is formatted directly, and since its shortest decimal
   form is `"-0"`, the result is `"-0"`.
5. The function is pure and safe for concurrent use.

Examples:

| `v` | result |
|---|---|
| `0` | `"0"` |
| `10.11` | `"10.11"` |
| `100` | `"100"` |
| `1000` | `"1,000"` |
| `100000` | `"100,000"` |
| `834142.32` | `"834,142.32"` |
| `10010000` | `"10,010,000"` |
| `123456789` | `"123,456,789"` |
| `999.5` | `"999.5"` |
| `-10` | `"-10"` |
| `-1000` | `"-1,000"` |
| `-10100000` | `"-10,100,000"` |
| `math.MaxFloat64` | see section 5 |
| `math.SmallestNonzeroFloat64` | `"0."` followed by 323 zeros and a final `5` |

## 3. Input specification

- `v`: any finite `float64` (negative, zero, positive; from
  `math.SmallestNonzeroFloat64` up to `math.MaxFloat64` in magnitude).
- NaN and infinities are outside the contract.

## 4. Output specification

- A `string` consisting of an optional leading `-`, the grouped integer
  part, and optionally `.` followed by the fractional digits.
- No exponent, no `+` sign, no trailing zeros in the fractional part (the
  shortest representation never has them), and no decimal point for
  integral values.

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- `0` gives `"0"`. Negative zero (`math.Copysign(0, -1)`) gives `"-0"`
  (rule 4: it is not below zero, but its shortest decimal form `"-0"`
  carries the sign; no comma is inserted).
- Values whose magnitude is below 1 have integer part `"0"`:
  `0.5` gives `"0.5"`, `-0.25` gives `"-0.25"`.
- Integer parts whose digit count is a multiple of three start with a full
  group: `123456.5` gives `"123,456.5"`.
- `math.MaxFloat64` must give
  `"179,769,313,486,231,570"` followed by 97 more groups `",000"`
  (309 integer digits in total).
- The function never panics for finite inputs.

# Functional specification: `func PluralWord(quantity int, singular, plural string) string`

## 1. Component overview

`PluralWord` is part of package `english` (`github.com/dustin/go-humanize/english`),
which builds user-friendly English text. It picks the singular or plural
form of a noun for a given quantity. When no explicit plural is supplied it
guesses the plural with a small set of regular English rules plus a few
technical special cases. `Plural(quantity, singular, plural)` in the same
file uses it to produce strings like `"42 objects"` and `"1,234,567 objects"`.
Keep the function simple: it only needs the regular rules and the listed
special cases, not a full English dictionary.

## 2. Functional requirements

Apply the following rules in this order; the first one that matches decides
the result.

1. **Quantity one.** If `quantity == 1`, return `singular` unchanged (even if
   `plural` is non-empty). Every other quantity, including `0` and negative
   values, needs the plural form.
2. **Explicit plural.** If `plural` is not the empty string, return `plural`
   unchanged.
3. **Special technical plurals.** If `singular` is exactly (case-sensitive)
   `"index"`, `"matrix"` or `"vertex"`, return `"indices"`, `"matrices"` or
   `"vertices"` respectively (the `specialPlurals` table in the context).
4. **Sibilant endings.** If `singular` ends with `"s"`, `"sh"`, `"tch"` or `"x"`
   (lower-case, case-sensitive), return `singular + "es"`. Note that a plain
   `"ch"` ending that is not `"tch"` does not match this rule
   (`"church"` gives `"churchs"`), and upper-case endings do not match
   (`"BOX"` gives `"BOXs"`).
5. **Consonant + o.** If `singular` has at least 2 bytes, its last byte is a
   lower-case `'o'`, and the byte before it is not a vowel, return
   `singular + "es"`. Vowels are exactly the ASCII letters `a e i o u` and
   `A E I O U` (`'y'` is not a vowel; any non-ASCII byte is not a vowel).
6. **Consonant + y.** If `singular` has at least 2 bytes, its last byte is a
   lower-case `'y'`, and the byte before it is not a vowel (same vowel set),
   return `singular` without its final `'y'` followed by `"ies"`.
7. **Default.** Otherwise return `singular + "s"`.

The function is pure and safe for concurrent use.

Examples (`plural` is `""` unless shown):

| quantity | singular | plural | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `"object"` | | `"object"` |
| 0 | `"object"` | | `"objects"` |
| -1 | `"object"` | | `"objects"` |
| 42 | `"object"` | | `"objects"` |
| 2 | `"vax"` | `"vaxen"` | `"vaxen"` |
| 1 | `"vax"` | `"vaxen"` | `"vax"` |
| 2 | `"index"` | | `"indices"` |
| 2 | `"Index"` | | `"Indexes"` |
| 2 | `"bus"` | | `"buses"` |
| 2 | `"bush"` | | `"bushes"` |
| 2 | `"watch"` | | `"watches"` |
| 2 | `"box"` | | `"boxes"` |
| 2 | `"hero"` | | `"heroes"` |
| 2 | `"radio"` | | `"radios"` |
| 2 | `"zoo"` | | `"zoos"` |
| 2 | `"lady"` | | `"ladies"` |
| 2 | `"day"` | | `"days"` |
| 2 | `"toy"` | | `"toys"` |

## 3. Input specification

- `quantity`: any `int`.
- `singular`: any string (may be empty, may contain non-ASCII UTF-8). Rules
  5 and 6 look at raw bytes, not runes.
- `plural`: any string; the empty string means "not given, guess it".

## 4. Output specification

- Returns a `string`: either `singular`, `plural`, a special plural, or
  `singular` with a suffix (`"es"`, `"s"`) or with its last `'y'` replaced by
  `"ies"`, as described above. No other transformation is applied (no case
  changes, no trimming).

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- Empty `singular` with no plural: `""` gives `"s"`.
- Single-character words are too short for rules 5 and 6: `"o"` gives
  `"os"`, `"y"` gives `"ys"`; but rule 4 still applies: `"s"` gives `"ses"`,
  `"x"` gives `"xes"`.
- Rule 3 is checked before rule 4: `"matrix"` gives `"matrices"`, not
  `"matrixes"`.
- Upper-case final `'O'` or `'Y'` does not trigger rules 5 or 6
  (`"HERO"` gives `"HEROs"`); upper-case vowels do count as vowels for the
  preceding byte (`"bAy"` gives `"bAys"`).
- A non-ASCII byte before a final `'o'` counts as a consonant:
  `"néo"` gives `"néoes"` (the byte before `'o'` is the last byte of the
  UTF-8 encoding of `é`).
- The function never panics.

## 1. Component overview

`stripTrailingZeros` is an unexported helper of the `humanize` package
(`github.com/dustin/go-humanize`), in `ftoa.go`. The package formats floats
with a fixed number of decimals (for example `strconv.FormatFloat(x, 'f', 6, 64)`
gives `"2.200000"`) and then calls this helper to remove the redundant zeros
at the end of the fractional part. `Ftoa`, `FtoaWithDigits`, `SI` and
`SIWithDigits` all depend on it: `Ftoa(2.2)` is `"2.2"`, `Ftoa(200)` is `"200"`,
`SI(2.2e-10, "F")` is `"220 pF"`.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. Remove every `'0'` character at the end of the fractional part of `s`
   (the part after the decimal point).
2. If, after that, the decimal point is the last character, remove the
   decimal point too. In that case the result is just the integer part.
3. Digits of the integer part (before the `.`) are never removed, even if they
   are zeros: `"200.000000"` gives `"200"`, `"100.0"` gives `"100"`.
4. Non-zero fractional digits are kept, including zeros that are followed by a
   non-zero digit: `"2.020000"` gives `"2.02"`, `"200.020000"` gives `"200.02"`.
5. The result is always a prefix of `s` (the function only shortens the
   string; it never adds or changes characters).
6. The function is pure and safe for concurrent use.

Examples:

| `s` | result |
|---|---|
| `"2.000000"` | `"2"` |
| `"2.200000"` | `"2.2"` |
| `"2.020000"` | `"2.02"` |
| `"200.000000"` | `"200"` |
| `"200.020000"` | `"200.02"` |
| `"2.234500"` | `"2.2345"` |
| `"0.000000"` | `"0"` |
| `"-0.000000"` | `"-0"` |
| `"-12.500"` | `"-12.5"` |
| `"7."` | `"7"` |
| `"1.23"` | `"1.23"` |

## 3. Input specification

- `s`: a decimal number in fixed-point notation, as produced by
  `strconv.FormatFloat(x, 'f', prec, 64)` with `prec >= 0` or a truncation of
  such a string at some fractional digit. Concretely: an optional leading
  `-`, one or more ASCII digits, a single `.`, then zero or more ASCII digits.
- The fractional part may be long (hundreds or thousands of digits) and may
  end in a long run of zeros.

## 4. Output specification

- A `string` that is a prefix of `s`, as described above. It never ends with
  `.` and, when it contains a `.`, never ends with `0`.

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- A fractional part made only of zeros (or empty) yields the integer part
  alone, with its sign: `"0.000000"` gives `"0"`, `"-0.000000"` gives `"-0"`,
  `"5."` gives `"5"`.
- A fraction with no trailing zeros is returned unchanged: `"3.14159"`.
- Only zeros directly at the end are affected; `"10.010"` gives `"10.01"`.
- The function never panics for inputs in the domain above.

# Functional specification: `func (r *Router) Match(req *http.Request, match *RouteMatch) bool`

## 1. Component overview

`(*Router).Match` belongs to the `mux` package (`github.com/gorilla/mux`, an
HTTP request router). It attempts to match a request against the router's
registered routes (and, through them, its subrouters). If a route matches, the
`Route`, `Handler` and `Vars` fields of `match` are filled and it returns
`true`. If no route matches, it returns `false` and records the reason in
`match.MatchErr`; if a handler is registered for that failure type
(`NotFoundHandler`, `MethodNotAllowedHandler`), that handler is put in
`match.Handler` and `true` is returned instead. `ServeHTTP` calls it and then
runs `match.Handler`; subrouters are matched by calling their `Match` from the
parent route.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. **Routes in registration order.** Call `route.Match(req, match)` for each
   route in `r.routes`, in order, passing the same `match`. Stop at the first
   route that returns `true`.
2. **Middleware on success.** When a route matched and `match.MatchErr` is
   `nil`, wrap `match.Handler` with the router's middlewares so that the
   middleware added **first** with `Use` is the **outermost** one: apply them
   from the last to the first, each time replacing `match.Handler` with
   `mw.Middleware(match.Handler)`. With middlewares `mw0, mw1` and route
   handler `h`, the final handler behaves as `mw0(mw1(h))`. When a route
   matched but `match.MatchErr` is non-nil (e.g. a subrouter answered with its
   own not-found handler and left `ErrNotFound`), the handler is **not**
   wrapped. In both cases return `true`.
3. **Method not allowed.** If no route matched and `match.MatchErr` is
   `ErrMethodMismatch` (some route matched everything except the method): if
   `r.MethodNotAllowedHandler` is non-nil, set `match.Handler` to it and
   return `true` (`MatchErr` stays `ErrMethodMismatch`); otherwise return
   `false` (with `MatchErr` still `ErrMethodMismatch`, `Handler` unchanged).
4. **Not found.** Otherwise, set `match.MatchErr = ErrNotFound`. If
   `r.NotFoundHandler` is non-nil, also set `match.Handler` to it and return
   `true`; else return `false`.
5. Middlewares are never applied to the not-found or method-not-allowed
   handlers.

|---|---|---|
| `Path("/products/")` named `stock` | `GET http://www.example.com/products/` | `true`, `Route` = that route, `MatchErr = nil` |
| same | `GET .../products` | `false`, `MatchErr = ErrNotFound`, `Handler = nil` |
| `Host("www.example.com").Subrouter()` with child `Path("/products/")` | `GET http://www.example.com/products/` | `true`, `Route` = the child route |
| `HandleFunc("/", h).Methods("GET","POST")` | `PUT /` | `false`, `MatchErr = ErrMethodMismatch` |

| `Methods("GET")` route, `MethodNotAllowedHandler = h405`, `NotFoundHandler = h404`, one middleware | `POST /` | `true`, `Handler = h405` (unwrapped), `MatchErr = ErrMethodMismatch` |

| `HandleFunc("/", h)`, `PathPrefix("/sub/").Subrouter()` with child `HandleFunc("/", h)` | `GET /sub/whatever` | `false`, `MatchErr = ErrNotFound` |
| same, subrouter has `NotFoundHandler = s404` | `GET /sub/whatever` | `true`, `Handler = s404`, `MatchErr = ErrNotFound`, no middleware applied |
| no routes, `NotFoundHandler = h404` | anything | `true`, `Handler = h404`, `MatchErr = ErrNotFound` |
| strict-slash route `Path("/111/")`, middlewares `mw0, mw1` | `GET /111` | `true`, `Handler` = `mw0(mw1(redirect to /111/))` |

## 3. Input specification

- `r`: a router with zero or more routes (possibly hundreds, possibly with
  subrouters), zero or more middlewares, and optional `NotFoundHandler` /
  `MethodNotAllowedHandler`.
- `req`: an `*http.Request` with non-nil `URL` and `Header`.
- `match`: non-nil; usually zero-valued (when called for a subrouter it holds
  the state of the parent's matching so far).

## 4. Output specification

- `bool` as described; `match` updated (`Route`, `Handler`, `Vars` by the
  matching route; `Handler` possibly wrapped by middlewares or set to a
  failure handler; `MatchErr` as described).

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- The router, its routes and the request are not modified.
- Middleware functions are invoked (to build the chain) once per successful
  match; the resulting handler is not executed by `Match`.
- Safe for concurrent use with distinct `match` values, provided the
  middleware functions are.

# Functional specification: `func matchMapWithRegex(toCheck map[string]*regexp.Regexp, toMatch map[string][]string, canonicalKey bool) bool`

## 1. Component overview

`matchMapWithRegex` belongs to the `mux` package (`github.com/gorilla/mux`, an
HTTP request router). It decides whether every required key of a multi-valued
map (such as an `http.Header`) carries a value accepted by a regular
expression. The route matcher created by
`Route.HeadersRegexp("Content-Type", "application/(text|json)", ...)` compiles
each pattern and calls `matchMapWithRegex(required, req.Header, true)`.

## 2. Functional requirements

Return `true` if and only if **every** entry `(k, re)` of `toCheck` is
satisfied by `toMatch`:

1. **Key lookup.** If `canonicalKey` is `true`, the key looked up in `toMatch`
   is `http.CanonicalHeaderKey(k)` (e.g. `"foo"` → `"Foo"`,
   `"x-requested-with"` → `"X-Requested-With"`); otherwise `k` is used exactly
   as given. The keys of `toMatch` are never transformed.
2. **Key must exist.** If the looked-up key is absent from `toMatch`, or maps
   to a `nil` slice, the entry is not satisfied.
3. **`nil` regexp = presence only.** If `re` is `nil`, the entry is satisfied
   as soon as the key exists with a non-`nil` slice (even an empty one).
4. **Otherwise at least one value must match.** If `re` is not `nil`, the entry
   is satisfied only if `re.MatchString(value)` is `true` for at least one
   value in the slice. Matching is the standard unanchored `regexp` search: a
   pattern matches if it matches any substring, unless the pattern itself uses
   `^`/`$` anchors. An empty (non-`nil`) slice therefore fails for a non-`nil`
   regexp, even one compiled from `""`.

An empty (or `nil`) `toCheck` yields `true`. Extra keys in `toMatch` and extra
values are ignored.

Examples (`canonicalKey = true`; patterns shown as their source text):

| `toCheck` | `toMatch` | result |
|---|---|---|
| `{"Accept": "html"}` | `{"Accept": ["text/plain", "text/html"]}` | `true` |
| `{"Accept": "html"}` | `{"Accept": ["application/xhtml+xml"]}` | `true` (substring) |
| `{"Origin": "^https://example.co$"}` | `{"Origin": ["https://example.co"]}` | `true` |
| `{"Origin": "^https://example.co$"}` | `{"Origin": ["https://example.co.uk"]}` | `false` |
| `{"foo": "ba[zr]"}` | `{"Foo": ["baz"]}` | `true` |
| `{"foo": "ba[zr]"}` | `{"Foo": ["bat"]}` | `false` |
| `{"foo": ""}` | `{"Foo": ["anything"]}` | `true` |
| `{"foo": ""}` | `{"Foo": []}` | `false` |
| `{"foo": nil}` | `{"Foo": []}` | `true` |
| `{"foo": nil}` | `{}` | `false` |
| `{"foo": "x"}`, `canonicalKey = false` | `{"Foo": ["x"]}` | `false` |
| `{}` | anything | `true` |

## 3. Input specification

- `toCheck`: required keys with compiled patterns (`*regexp.Regexp`, possibly
  `nil`); may be `nil` or empty; up to a few hundred entries; keys in any case.
- `toMatch`: available values per key (typically an `http.Header`); may be
  `nil`; slices may hold dozens of values.
- `canonicalKey`: whether `toCheck` keys must be canonicalised as MIME header
  keys before lookup.

## 4. Output specification

- `bool` as described in section 2. The result does not depend on map
  iteration order.

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- Neither map nor any regexp is modified.
- Only keys are canonicalised; values are passed to the regexp unchanged.
- Never panics for valid inputs; safe for concurrent use as long as the maps
  are not written concurrently (compiled regexps are safe to share).

# Functional specification: `func matchMapWithString(toCheck map[string]string, toMatch map[string][]string, canonicalKey bool) bool`

## 1. Component overview

`matchMapWithString` belongs to the `mux` package (`github.com/gorilla/mux`, an
HTTP request router). It decides whether a set of required key/value pairs is
present in a multi-valued map such as an `http.Header`. The route matcher
created by `Route.Headers("Content-Type", "application/json", ...)` calls it as
`matchMapWithString(required, req.Header, true)`, so a route only matches a
request whose headers contain every required pair.

## 2. Functional requirements

Return `true` if and only if **every** entry `(k, v)` of `toCheck` is satisfied
by `toMatch`:

1. **Key lookup.** If `canonicalKey` is `true`, the key looked up in `toMatch`
   is `http.CanonicalHeaderKey(k)` (e.g. `"x-requested-with"` →
   `"X-Requested-With"`); otherwise `k` is used exactly as given. The keys of
   `toMatch` are never transformed.
2. **Key must exist.** If the looked-up key is absent from `toMatch`, or maps
   to a `nil` slice, the entry is not satisfied.
3. **Empty required value = presence only.** If `v` is `""`, the entry is
   satisfied as soon as the key exists with a non-`nil` slice (even an empty,
   non-`nil` slice).
4. **Otherwise exact membership.** If `v` is not empty, the entry is satisfied
   only if at least one string in the slice is exactly equal to `v`
   (case-sensitive, no trimming, no pattern matching: `"ba[zr]"` does not match
   `"bar"`).

An empty (or `nil`) `toCheck` yields `true`. Extra keys in `toMatch` and extra
values in a slice are ignored.

Examples (`canonicalKey = true` unless noted):

| `toCheck` | `toMatch` | result |
|---|---|---|
| `{"x-requested-with": "XMLHttpRequest"}` | `{"X-Requested-With": ["XMLHttpRequest"]}` | `true` |
| `{"x-requested-with": ""}` | `{"X-Requested-With": ["anything"]}` | `true` |
| `{"x-requested-with": "XMLHttpRequest"}` | `{}` | `false` |
| `{"x-requested-with": "a"}`, `canonicalKey = false` | `{"X-Requested-With": ["a"]}` | `false` |
| `{"foo": "bar", "baz": "ding"}`, `false` | `{"foo": ["bar"], "baz": ["dong"]}` | `false` |
| `{"foo": "bar", "baz": "ding"}`, `false` | `{"foo": ["x", "bar"], "baz": ["ding"]}` | `true` |
| `{"k": ""}` | `{"K": []}` (non-nil, empty) | `true` |
| `{}` | anything | `true` |

## 3. Input specification

- `toCheck`: required pairs; may be `nil` or empty; keys may be in any letter
  case; values may be `""`. Up to a few hundred entries.
- `toMatch`: the available values per key (typically an `http.Header`, whose
  keys are already canonical). May be `nil`. Slices may hold dozens of values.
- `canonicalKey`: whether the `toCheck` keys must be canonicalised as MIME
  header keys before lookup.

## 4. Output specification

- `bool` as described in section 2. The result does not depend on map
  iteration order.

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- Neither map is modified.
- Value comparison is exact; only keys are canonicalised (and only when
  `canonicalKey` is set).
- Pure function apart from reading the maps; never panics; safe for concurrent
  use as long as the maps are not being written concurrently.

# Functional specification: `func (r *routeRegexp) getURLQuery(req *http.Request) string`

## 1. Component overview

`getURLQuery` belongs to the `mux` package (`github.com/gorilla/mux`, an HTTP
request router). A route created with `Queries("foo", "{v1}")` owns one
`routeRegexp` of type `regexpTypeQuery` per key/value pair, with template
`"foo={v1}"` (see the *Instance state* section of the context). To match such a
template, the router does not look at the whole query string: it extracts the
single parameter named by the template from the request URL and renders it as
`key=value`. `getURLQuery` performs this extraction; its result is then matched
against the template's regexp (e.g. `^foo=(?P<v0>.*)$`) and used to extract
route variables.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. **Non-query templates.** If `r.regexpType` is not `regexpTypeQuery`, return
   `""` without inspecting the request.
2. **Template key.** The key is the part of `r.template` before the first `=`
   (`"foo={v1}"` → `"foo"`, `"foo="` → `"foo"`). It is used exactly as written
   (it is not unescaped).
3. **Request parameters.** Parse the request's raw query with
   `req.URL.Query()` (standard `net/url` parsing: pairs separated by `&` (and
   `;` in this Go version), `+` and percent-escapes decoded in keys and values,
   a pair without `=` has the empty value, pairs with invalid escapes are
   dropped).
4. **Result.** If the parsed query contains the template key with at least one
   value, return `key + "=" + firstValue`, where `firstValue` is the
   **decoded** value of the first occurrence of that key in the query string.
   Otherwise return `""`.
5. Only exact key equality counts (`"fffoo"` is not `"foo"`; keys are
   case-sensitive).

Examples (template → raw query → result):

| template | raw query | result |
|---|---|---|
| `foo=bar` | `foo=bar&baz=ding` | `"foo=bar"` |
| `baz=ding` | `foo=bar&baz=dong` | `"baz=dong"` |
| `foo={v1}` | `bar=2&foo=1` | `"foo=1"` |
| `foo=` | `` (empty) | `""` |
| `foo=` | `foo=` | `"foo="` |
| `foo=` | `foo` | `"foo="` |
| `foo=bar` | `fffoo=bar&baz=dingggg` | `""` |
| `foo={v1}` | `foo=%25bar%26%20%2F%3D%3F` | `"foo=%bar& /=?"` |
| `foo={v1}` | `foo=a&foo=b` | `"foo=a"` |
| `foo={v1}` | `foo=a+b` | `"foo=a b"` |
| `foo={v1}` | `foo=%zz&foo=2` | `"foo=2"` (invalid pair dropped) |
| `f o={v1}` | `f+o=1` | `"f o=1"` |
| `/foo` (path type) | `foo=bar` | `""` |

## 3. Input specification

- `r`: a `routeRegexp` built by `newRouteRegexp`; query templates always
  contain `=`.
- `req`: an `*http.Request` with non-nil `URL`; only `req.URL.RawQuery` is
  relevant. Query strings may hold from zero to several hundred parameters,
  with repeated keys and percent-encoded or `+`-encoded characters.

## 4. Output specification

- A `string`: `""` or `key=value` with the decoded value, as above.

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- `r` and `req` are not modified (the URL's raw query is only read).
- The value is returned decoded and is not re-escaped.
- Safe for concurrent use.

## 1. Component overview

`setMatch` belongs to the `mux` package (`github.com/gorilla/mux`, an HTTP
request router). Once `(*Route).Match` has decided that route `r` matches a
request, it calls `r.regexp.setMatch(req, match, r)` to fill
`match.Vars` with the route variables taken from the request's host, path and
query string, and, for strict-slash routes, to install a redirect handler when
the request's trailing slash differs from the template's. The receiver `v` is
the route's group of templates (`host`, `path`, `queries`; each a
`*routeRegexp`, see the context). For example, the route
`Host("{v1}.domain.com").Path("/{v2}/{v3}").Queries("foo", "{v4}")` and the
request `http://aaa.domain.com/bbb/ccc?foo=ddd` yield
`Vars = {v1: aaa, v2: bbb, v3: ccc, v4: ddd}`.

## 2. Functional requirements

`m.Vars` is a non-nil map supplied by the caller; variables are added to it
(existing entries with other names are kept, same names are overwritten).

1. **Host variables.** If `v.host` is non-nil, take the request host
   (`getHost(req)`: `req.URL.Host` for absolute URLs, else `req.Host`) and
   search it with `v.host.regexp`. If it matches, store each host variable
   (`v.host.varsN[i]`) with the text captured by its group. If it does not
   match, store nothing for the host.
2. **Path.** The path used is `req.URL.Path`, or `req.URL.EscapedPath()` if
   the **route** `r` has `useEncodedPath` set (the route's flag, not the
   template's option, decides). If `v.path` is non-nil and its regexp matches
   this path, store the path variables the same way. Otherwise nothing is
   stored for the path and no redirect is considered.
3. **Strict-slash redirect.** Only when the path matched and
   `v.path.options.strictSlash` is `true`: let *A* = "the path used in rule 2
   ends with `/`" and *B* = "`v.path.template` ends with `/`". If *A* ≠ *B*,
   set `m.Handler` to `http.RedirectHandler(target, http.StatusMovedPermanently)`
   where `target` is obtained by parsing `req.URL.String()` with `url.Parse`,
   then removing the final `/` from its `Path` (when *A*) or appending `/` to
   it (when *B*), and rendering it again with `String()`. Scheme, host, query
   and fragment are preserved: `http://localhost/foo/123/?a=b#frag` against
   template `/{arg1}/{arg2:[0-9]+}` redirects to
   `http://localhost/foo/123?a=b#frag`. If *A* = *B*, `m.Handler` is left
   unchanged. Prefix templates never have `strictSlash` set.
4. **Query variables.** For each query template `q` in `v.queries`, in order,
   take `q.getURLQuery(req)` (e.g. `"foo=ddd"`) and search it with `q.regexp`;
   if it matches, store `q`'s variables from it (values are therefore
   decoded: `?foo=%25bar%26%20%2F%3D%3F` with `foo={v1}` gives
   `v1 = "%bar& /=?"`). Non-matching query templates store nothing.

   others from being processed. Nothing else in `m` is changed.

| `Path("/111/")`, strict | `http://localhost/111/` | `{}` | unchanged (nil) |
| `Path("/{arg1}/{arg2:[0-9]+}/")`, strict | `http://localhost/foo/123` | `{arg1: foo, arg2: 123}` | redirect to `http://localhost/foo/123/` |
| `PathPrefix("/static/")`, strict router | `http://localhost/static/logo.png` | `{}` | unchanged |
| `Path("/v1/{v1}/v2")`, route uses encoded path | `http://localhost/v1/1%2F2/v2` | `{v1: 1%2F2}` | unchanged |
| `Path("/v1/{v1}/v2")`, decoded path | same request | `{}` (path `/v1/1/2/v2` does not match) | unchanged |

| `Queries("foo", "{v1}", "baz", "{v2}")` | `?foo=bar&baz=ding` | `{v1: bar, v2: ding}` | unchanged |

- `v`: the route's template group (`host`, `path` may be nil; `queries` may be
  empty). Templates may carry up to a few hundred variables.
- `req`: a request with non-nil `URL` (absolute or relative). Callers guarantee

  does not check the error and panics with a nil-pointer dereference there).

- `r`: the route that owns `v`; only `r.useEncodedPath` is consulted.

## 4. Output specification

- No return value. Effects: entries added to `m.Vars`; possibly `m.Handler`
  replaced by a 301 redirect handler (rule 3).

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- `req`, `v` and `r` are not modified.
- Variable values are the raw captured substrings (no decoding of the path or
  host; query values come already decoded from the query parsing).
- When several templates define the same name, later parts (path after host,
  queries after path) overwrite earlier ones.

# Functional specification: `func (r *routeRegexp) url(values map[string]string) (string, error)`

## 1. Component overview

`url` belongs to the `mux` package (`github.com/gorilla/mux`, an HTTP request
router). A `routeRegexp` is the compiled form of one route template (a host,
path, path-prefix or query template; see the *Instance state* section of the
context). `url` performs **reverse routing** for that template: it fills the
template's variables with the given values and returns the resulting URL part.
`Route.URL`, `Route.URLHost` and `Route.URLPath` call it for the route's host,
path and each query template, e.g. route
`Host("{subdomain}.domain.com").Path("/articles/{category}/{id:[0-9]+}")`
with values `subdomain=foo, category=technology, id=42` builds
`http://foo.domain.com/articles/technology/42`.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. **All variables are required.** For each variable name in `r.varsN`, in
   order, look it up in `values`. If a name is missing from the map (a present
   key with value `""` counts as present), return `""` and an error whose
   message is exactly `mux: missing route variable "<name>"` (the name quoted
   as with Go's `%q`). The first missing name in `varsN` order is reported.
   Keys of `values` that are not variables of this template are ignored.
2. **Query values are escaped.** For a query template (`regexpTypeQuery`),
   each value is escaped with `url.QueryEscape` before substitution (space →
   `+`, `%` → `%25`, `&` → `%26`, `/` → `%2F`, `=` → `%3D`, `?` → `%3F`). For
   host, path and prefix templates values are inserted verbatim.
3. **Substitution.** The result is the template with every `{...}` token
   replaced by its (possibly escaped) value and all literal text unchanged; it
   has the same shape as `r.reverse` with the values filled in. Templates
   without variables yield their literal text (`"/111/"` → `"/111/"`,
   `"foo="` → `"foo="`, `""` → `""`).
4. **Validation.** If the substituted string matches the whole-template
   regexp `r.regexp`, return it with a `nil` error. Otherwise check each
   variable's **raw, unescaped** value against its own validator `r.varsR[k]`,
   in `varsN` order; for the first one that does not match, return `""` and an
   error with message exactly
   `mux: variable "<value>" doesn't match, expected "<validator>"`, where both
   parts are quoted as with `%q` and `<validator>` is `r.varsR[k].String()`
   (e.g. `^[0-9]+$`). If every individual value matches its validator (this
   can happen when escaping changed the value), return the substituted string
   with a `nil` error even though the whole regexp did not match.

Examples:

| template (type) | values | result |
|---|---|---|
| `/articles/{category}/{id:[0-9]+}` (path) | category=technology, id=42 | `"/articles/technology/42"`, nil |
| same | category=technology, id=x | `""`, `mux: variable "x" doesn't match, expected "^[0-9]+$"` |
| same | category=technology | `""`, `mux: missing route variable "id"` |
| `{v1:[a-z]+}.google.com` (host) | v1=Bad | `""`, `mux: variable "Bad" doesn't match, expected "^[a-z]+$"` |
| `{a}.{b}` (host) | a=x.y, b=z | `""`, `mux: variable "x.y" doesn't match, expected "^[^.]+$"` |
| `/a/{v1}` (path) | v1=x/y | `""`, `mux: variable "x/y" doesn't match, expected "^[^/]+$"` |
| `/{a:[0-9]+}/{b:[0-9]+}` | a=x, b=y | error names `"x"` (first in order) |
| `/{v1}/` (path, strict slash) | v1=x | `"/x/"`, nil |
| `/static/` (prefix) | none | `"/static/"`, nil |
| `foo={v1}` (query) | v1=`%bar& /=?` | `"foo=%25bar%26+%2F%3D%3F"`, nil |
| `foo={v1:[0-9]+}` (query) | v1=`1 0` | `""`, `mux: variable "1 0" doesn't match, expected "^[0-9]+$"` |
| `foo={v1:[a-z ]+}` (query) | v1=`a b` | `"foo=a+b"`, nil (raw value is valid) |

## 3. Input specification

- `r`: a `routeRegexp` produced by `newRouteRegexp` (fields as described in
  the context). Templates contain from zero to a few hundred variables and
  never contain the character `%`.
- `values`: variable name → value; may be `nil` (only valid when the template
  has no variables) and may contain extra keys. Values are arbitrary strings.

## 4. Output specification

- `(string, nil)` on success; `("", error)` on failure with the exact messages
  above (tests compare built URLs; error text is created with `fmt.Errorf`).

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

- `r` and `values` are not modified.
- A value of `""` is present, not missing; it then fails validation unless the
  variable's pattern accepts the empty string.
- No escaping is applied to path/host values (`"1%2F2"` is inserted as is).
- Safe for concurrent use.

# Functional specification: `func (r *Route) Queries(pairs ...string) *Route`

## 1. Component overview

`Queries` belongs to the `mux` package (`github.com/gorilla/mux`, an HTTP
request router). It is part of the fluent route-building API: it adds matchers
for URL query parameters to the route and returns the route so calls can be
chained, e.g.

```go
r := mux.NewRouter()
r.Path("/api").Queries("foo", "bar", "id", "{id:[0-9]+}")
```

This route only matches requests whose URL contains `foo=bar` and an `id`
parameter made of digits (e.g. `?foo=bar&id=42`); `id` becomes a route
variable. Errors are not returned directly: like every builder method, they
are recorded in the route's `err` field (visible through `GetError()`), after
which the route never matches.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. **Arguments are key/value pairs.** `pairs` is read as
   `key1, value1, key2, value2, ...`.
2. **Odd count.** If the number of strings is odd, set `r.err` to an error with
   message `mux: number of parameters must be multiple of 2, got <pairs>`,
   where `<pairs>` is the slice formatted with `%v` (e.g.
   `mux: number of parameters must be multiple of 2, got [foo bar baz]`),
   add no matcher, and return **`nil`** (not the route). This happens even
   if the route already had an error.
3. **One query template per pair.** Otherwise, for each pair in order, build
   the template `key + "=" + value` and register it on the route as a
   query-type template (`regexpTypeQuery`) via `addRegexpMatcher` (see context).
   The result of each registration is stored in `r.err` (so a successful
   registration leaves `r.err == nil`). As soon as one registration yields an
   error, stop: later pairs are not registered (pairs registered before it
   stay registered), and return `r`.
4. **Existing error.** If the route already has an error, the registration
   helper reports that same error; `r.err` keeps it, nothing is added, and `r`
   is returned.
5. **Return value.** In all non-odd cases return the receiver `r`. With zero
   arguments nothing changes and `r` is returned.

Resulting templates (as reported by `GetQueriesTemplates()`) and regexps (as
reported by `GetQueriesRegexp()`):

# Functional specification: `func (r *Route) Match(req *http.Request, match *RouteMatch) bool`

## 1. Component overview

`(*Route).Match` belongs to the `mux` package (`github.com/gorilla/mux`, an
HTTP request router). A route is a list of matchers (host/path/query
templates, methods, headers, schemes, custom functions, subrouters) added with
the fluent builder API. `(*Router).Match` calls `route.Match(req, &match)` for
each registered route in turn until one returns `true`; the same
`RouteMatch` value is passed to every route, so its `MatchErr` carries
information between routes (e.g. "some route matched everything except the
HTTP method", which lets the router answer 405 instead of 404). On success the
match receives the route, its handler and the route variables.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. **Unusable routes.** If the route is build-only (`r.buildOnly`) or has a
   build error (`r.err != nil`), return `false` without touching `match`.
2. **Run every matcher in order.** Call `m.Match(req, match)` for each
   matcher `m` in `r.matchers`:
   - If a matcher of type `methodMatcher` fails, remember a method mismatch
     and **continue** with the next matchers.
   - If any other matcher fails: if `match.MatchErr` is currently
     `ErrNotFound` (left there, e.g., by a subrouter that found nothing), reset
     it to `nil`; forget any remembered method mismatch; return `false`
     immediately. (Any other `MatchErr` value, including `ErrMethodMismatch`
     set earlier, is left as is.)
3. **Only the method failed.** If all non-method matchers succeeded but a
   method matcher failed, set `match.MatchErr = ErrMethodMismatch` and return
   `false` (no other field is changed).
4. **Full match.** Otherwise the route matches:
   1. If `match.MatchErr` is `ErrMethodMismatch` (an earlier route matched
      everything but the method), set `match.MatchErr = nil` and set
      `match.Handler = r.handler`, overriding any handler already there.
      Any other `MatchErr` value (e.g. `ErrNotFound`) is left unchanged.
   2. If `match.Route` is `nil`, set it to `r` (a route already set — e.g. by
      a subrouter matcher — is kept).
   3. If `match.Handler` is `nil`, set it to `r.handler`.
   4. If `match.Vars` is `nil`, set it to a new empty map.
   5. Call `setMatch` on the route's template group (`r.regexp`), passing the request, the match and the route itself, to add the route variables (and

   6. Return `true`.

| `Methods("GET").Path("/a")` | `PUT /b`, `MatchErr = ErrNotFound` | `false`, `MatchErr = nil` |
| `Methods("GET").Path("/a")` | `PUT /b`, `MatchErr = ErrMethodMismatch` | `false`, still `ErrMethodMismatch` |
| `Path("/a")` | `GET /a`, `MatchErr = ErrMethodMismatch`, `Handler = h0` | `true`, `MatchErr = nil`, `Handler = r.handler`, `Route = r`, `Vars = {}` |
| `Path("/a")` | `GET /a`, `MatchErr = ErrNotFound` | `true`, `MatchErr` stays `ErrNotFound`, `Route = r` |

# Functional specification: `func (r *Route) URL(pairs ...string) (*url.URL, error)`

## 1. Component overview

`URL` belongs to the `mux` package (`github.com/gorilla/mux`, an HTTP request
router). It performs **reverse routing**: given values for the route's
variables, it builds the URL that the route would match. Example:

```go
r := mux.NewRouter()
r.Host("{subdomain}.domain.com").
  Path("/articles/{category}/{id:[0-9]+}").
  Name("article")
u, err := r.Get("article").URL("subdomain", "news", "category", "technology", "id", "42")
// u.String() == "http://news.domain.com/articles/technology/42", err == nil
```

A route may have a host template (`r.regexp.host`), a path or path-prefix
template (`r.regexp.path`), and any number of query templates
(`r.regexp.queries`), each a `*routeRegexp` able to fill in its own variables
with `url(values)` (see context).

## 2. Functional requirements

1. **Route error.** If `r.err` is non-nil, return `nil` and `r.err` itself.
2. **Variables.** Turn `pairs` (`name, value, name, value, ...`) into the
   variable map using `r.prepareVars(pairs...)` (which also applies the
   route's `BuildVarsFunc`, if any). If that fails (odd number of strings),
   return `nil` and its error unchanged (message
   `mux: number of parameters must be multiple of 2, got [x]` for `URL("x")`).
3. **Host.** If the route has a host template, build the host with its
   `url(values)`; on error return `nil` and that error. When a host exists,
   the scheme is the route's `buildScheme` if non-empty, else `"http"`.
   Without a host template, the scheme stays empty even if `Schemes(...)` was
   called.
4. **Path.** If the route has a path (or path-prefix) template, build the path
   with its `url(values)`; on error return `nil` and that error.
5. **Queries.** For each query template, in registration order, build its
   `key=value` part with `url(values)`; on the first error return `nil` and
   that error. Join the parts with `&` to form the raw query (empty when there
   are no query templates).
6. **Order of failures.** Host is built first, then path, then queries; the
   first failing part's error is returned.
7. **Result.** On success return a new `*url.URL` with exactly these fields set:
   `Scheme`, `Host`, `Path`, `RawQuery` (all others zero). Extra names in
   `pairs` are ignored.

Examples (`u.String()` shown):

| route | pairs | result |
|---|---|---|
| `Host("foo.domain.com")` | none | `http://foo.domain.com` |
| `Host("{subdomain}.domain.com")` | subdomain=bar | `http://bar.domain.com` |
| `Host("foo.domain.com").Path("/articles")` | none | `http://foo.domain.com/articles` |
| `Path("/articles/{category}/{id:[0-9]+}")` | category=technology, id=42 | `/articles/technology/42` |
| `Schemes("https", "ftp").Host("localhost")` | none | `https://localhost` |
| `Path("/a").Schemes("https")` | none | `/a` (no host → no scheme) |
| `Host("www.example.com").Path("/api").Queries("foo", "bar", "baz", "ding")` | none | `http://www.example.com/api?foo=bar&baz=ding` |
| `Queries("foo", "{v1}", "bar", "", "baz", "lit")` | v1=`a b` | `?foo=a+b&bar=&baz=lit` (RawQuery `foo=a+b&bar=&baz=lit`) |
| `Path("/a/{x}")` | x=1, x=2 | `/a/2` |
| `PathPrefix("/static/")` | none | `/static/` |
| route with no templates | none | `""` (empty URL) |

v1=1 → `mux: missing route variable "h"`; `Path("/articles/{category}/{id:[0-9]+}")`

## 1. Component overview

`NewConstraint` belongs to the `semver` package
(`github.com/Masterminds/semver/v3`). It parses a version-constraint
expression such as `">= 1.2.3, < 2.0 || ^3"` into a `*Constraints` value that
versions can then be checked against (`Check`, `Validate`) or printed
(`String`). The expression language:

- **OR groups** are separated by `||`.
- Inside a group, **AND-ed constraints** are separated by commas and/or
  whitespace (`">= 1.2.3, < 2.0"`, `">= 1.2.3 < 2.0"` and even `">1<2"` all
  give two constraints). A trailing comma is accepted; a leading one is not.
- Each constraint is an optional operator (`=`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `=>`,
  `<=`, `=<`, `~`, `~>`, `^`, or none) followed by a version that may be
  partial or contain wildcards (`1`, `1.2`, `1.x`, `1.2.*`, `*`), may start
  with `v`, and may carry a pre-release and metadata.
- **Hyphen ranges** `A - B` (whitespace on both sides of the `-`) mean
  `>= A, <= B`. A `-` without surrounding whitespace is a pre-release
  separator, so `"1.1-3"` is one constraint (version 1.1 with pre-release `3`).

The helpers and regular expressions listed in the context (`rewriteRange`,
`parseConstraint`, `validConstraintRegex`, `findConstraintRegex`) define the
exact grammar and are meant to be used.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. **Range rewrite.** First rewrite every hyphen range in the whole input
   exactly as `rewriteRange` does (e.g. `"3 - 4 || => 3.0, < 4"` becomes
   `">= 3, <= 4|| => 3.0, < 4"`).
2. **OR split.** Split the rewritten string on every occurrence of `"||"`.
   Each piece is an OR segment, kept verbatim (surrounding whitespace is not
   trimmed). Segments are processed in order, left to right.
3. **Segment validation.** A segment is valid when it matches
   `validConstraintRegex` in full. For the first invalid segment, return
   `nil` and an error whose message is `"improper constraint: "` followed by
   the segment verbatim (for example `">= 1.2 || foo"` fails with
   `"improper constraint:  foo"`, with two spaces).
4. **Constraint extraction.** In a valid segment, take every non-overlapping
   match of `findConstraintRegex`, left to right; each match is one AND-ed
   constraint, parsed with `parseConstraint`. If `parseConstraint` fails
   (e.g. `">=1.2.3-01"`, a numeric pre-release with a leading zero, or a
   component too large for `uint64`), return `nil` and that error unchanged
   (its message is `"constraint Parser Error"`). Earlier segments are fully
   processed before later ones are validated, so the first problem in
   left-to-right order is the one reported.
5. **Result.** On success return `&Constraints{...}` whose `constraints`
   field has one entry per OR segment, in order, each being the list of
   parsed `*constraint` values of that segment, in order, and a `nil` error.

## 3. Input specification

- `c`: any string. Real inputs range from a single constraint to long
  expressions with dozens of constraints and several OR groups, with varied
  spacing.

## 4. Output specification

- Success: non-nil `*Constraints`, `nil` error. Every inner list is non-empty
  and every `*constraint` is exactly what `parseConstraint` returns for the
  corresponding match (operator, original text, version, wildcard flags).
- Failure: `nil` and a non-nil `error` with one of the two messages above.

## 5. Edge cases and constraints

| input | result (groups x constraints, or error) |
|---|---|
| `">= 1.1"` | 1 group, 1 constraint |
| `">40.50.60, < 50.70"` | 1 group, 2 constraints |
| `"2.0"`, `"v2.3.5-20161202202307-sha.e8fc5e5"`, `"1.1-3"` | 1 group, 1 constraint |
| `">= 1.2.3 < 2.0"`, `">= 1.2.3, < 2.0"`, `">1<2"`, `">=1.2.3,"` | 1 group (2, 2, 2, 1 constraints) |

| `">= bar"`, `"BAR >= 1.2.3"`, `"foo"`, `",>=1.2.3"` | error `improper constraint: <segment>` |

# Functional specification: `func StrictNewVersion(v string) (*Version, error)`

## 1. Component overview

`StrictNewVersion` belongs to the `semver` package
(`github.com/Masterminds/semver/v3`). It parses a string that must be a
complete Semantic Version 2.0.0 — `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, optionally followed by
`-PRERELEASE` and/or `+METADATA` — into a `*Version` (fields described under
"Instance state of `Version`" in the context). Unlike the lenient `NewVersion`
it does not coerce: no leading `v`, no missing components. It is meant to be
fast (callers use it on hot paths), so avoid needless work and allocations.

## 2. Functional requirements

**Splitting.** Conceptually the input is cut at its first two `.` characters
into three pieces: major, minor, and a *tail* (everything after the second
dot). Only the tail may carry a pre-release or metadata:

1. If the tail contains a `+`, everything after the **first** `+` is the
   metadata and is removed from the tail.
2. Then, if the remaining tail contains a `-`, everything after the **first**
   `-` is the pre-release and is removed from the tail. (So a `-` inside the
   metadata is never mistaken for a pre-release: `1.2.3+b-c` has metadata
   `b-c` and no pre-release; `1.2.3-a-b+c-d` has pre-release `a-b` and
   metadata `c-d`.)
3. What remains of the tail is the patch piece.

**Checks, in this order; the first failure is returned with a `nil` version:**

1. Empty input -> `ErrEmptyString`.
2. Fewer than two `.` characters (fewer than three pieces) -> `ErrInvalidSemVer`.
   Extra dots after the second one end up in the tail (`1.2.3.4` has the
   patch piece `3.4`).
3. For the major, then the minor, then the patch piece (finish all checks on
   one piece before the next): if it contains any character other than ASCII
   `0`-`9` -> `ErrInvalidCharacters`; else if it is longer than one character
   and starts with `0` -> `ErrSegmentStartsZero`.
4. Convert major, minor, patch to `uint64` with `strconv.ParseUint(piece, 10, 64)`;
   if that fails (empty piece such as in `1..3`, or a value above
   18446744073709551615), return the error from `strconv` unchanged.
5. If the pre-release is non-empty, check its `.`-separated identifiers in
   order: an identifier made only of digits that is longer than one character
   and starts with `0` -> `ErrSegmentStartsZero`; otherwise an identifier
   containing a character outside `[0-9A-Za-z-]` -> `ErrInvalidPrerelease`.
6. If the metadata is non-empty, any of its `.`-separated identifiers
   containing a character outside `[0-9A-Za-z-]` -> `ErrInvalidMetadata`
   (leading zeros are allowed in metadata).

Empty identifiers (e.g. `1.2.3-a..b`) are **not** rejected, and a bare
trailing `-` or `+` simply yields an empty pre-release / metadata
(`1.2.3-`, `1.2.3+` and `1.2.3-+` all parse as 1.2.3).

**Success.** Return a new `*Version` with `major`, `minor`, `patch` set to the
parsed numbers, `pre` and `metadata` set to the extracted strings (without
the `-` / `+`; `""` when absent), `original` set to the input string exactly,
and a `nil` error.

## 3. Input specification

- `v`: any string, possibly empty, possibly containing non-ASCII characters,
  whitespace or newlines. Valid inputs may have long pre-release / metadata
  parts (dozens of identifiers).

## 4. Output specification

- On success: non-nil `*Version`, `nil` error.
- On failure: `nil` version and a non-nil error; one of the package error
  variables listed in the context, or the `strconv` error from step 4.

| `"1.2.3"` | 1.2.3 |
| `"1.2.3+test.01"` | 1.2.3, metadata `test.01` |

# Functional specification: `func comparePrerelease(v, o string) int`

## 1. Component overview

`comparePrerelease` belongs to the `semver` package
(`github.com/Masterminds/semver/v3`). It orders two pre-release strings by
Semantic Versioning precedence. A pre-release string is the part of a version
after the `-` and before any `+`, without the `-` itself, e.g. `"beta.2"` in
`"4.2.0-beta.2+build.7"`. It consists of identifiers separated by `.`.

`(*Version).Compare` calls it when two versions have equal major, minor and
patch and both have a non-empty pre-release; constraint checks also call it
(sometimes with an empty string on one or both sides). It therefore decides
results such as `4.2.0-alpha < 4.2.0-beta`, `3.2.0-beta.4 > 3.2.0-beta.2` and
`7.43.0-SNAPSHOT.99 < 7.43.0-SNAPSHOT.103`.

## 2. Functional requirements

Return `-1` if `v` has lower precedence than `o`, `1` if higher, `0` if equal.

1. **Identifiers.** Split each string on every `.` into a list of
   identifiers. Empty identifiers are kept (`""` is a list with one empty
   identifier; `"a."` is `["a", ""]`).
2. **Position by position.** Compare the identifiers at position 0, 1, 2, ...
   up to the length of the longer list. When one list is shorter, its missing
   positions count as the empty identifier `""`. The first position whose
   identifiers differ in precedence decides the result. If no position decides
   it, return `0`.
3. **Comparing two identifiers `a` (from `v`) and `b` (from `o`):**
   1. If `a` and `b` are the same string, they are equal (move on).
   2. Otherwise, an empty identifier is lower than a non-empty one.
   3. An identifier is *numeric* when it is a valid unsigned base-10
      integer that fits in a `uint64`: only ASCII digits, at least one digit,
      no sign, value at most 18446744073709551615. Anything else, including
      `"-2"`, `"beta2"` and digit strings that overflow `uint64`, is
      *alphanumeric*.
   4. A numeric identifier is lower than an alphanumeric one.
   5. Two alphanumeric identifiers are ordered by plain byte-wise string
      comparison (Go `<` on strings: `"-"` < digits < upper-case < lower-case).
   6. Two numeric identifiers are ordered by integer value. If the values
      are equal but the strings differ (leading zeros, e.g. `"01"` and `"1"`),
      the result is `-1` whichever side is which.

Examples:

| `v` | `o` | result |
|---|---|---|
| `"beta"` | `"beta"` | `0` |

# Functional specification

## 1. Component overview

`Base32.encode(byte[] in, int inPos, int inAvail, Context context)` is the incremental (streaming) encoder of the `Base32` codec. It is called repeatedly with successive chunks of input bytes, and once with `inAvail < 0` to signal the end of the input. The encoded text is accumulated in the `context` object (see "Instance state"); the method returns nothing.

## 2. Functional requirements

1. If `context.eof` is already `true`, return immediately without any change.
2. **Data call** (`inAvail >= 0`): consume the `inAvail` bytes `in[inPos .. inPos+inAvail-1]`. Bytes are treated as unsigned (0..255). The call may begin in the middle of a 5-byte group: the `context` remembers how many bytes of the current group have been seen (`context.modulus`, cycling 0..4) and their accumulated bits, so that the output is the same regardless of how the input is split into calls. Each time a complete group of 5 input bytes has been collected, 8 output characters are appended to `context.buffer` (at `context.pos`, which advances), each representing 5 bits of the group, most significant bits first, taken from the 32-character Base32 alphabet (`A-Z 2-7`) or the extended-hex alphabet (`0-9 A-V`) as selected by the instance. `context.currentLinePos` counts the characters written on the current line; after each group of 8 characters, if the instance uses line chunking (`lineLength > 0`) and `currentLinePos` has reached `lineLength`, the line separator bytes of the instance are appended and `currentLinePos` is reset to 0.
3. **End-of-input call** (`inAvail < 0`): set `context.eof = true`. Then, if no bytes are pending (`context.modulus == 0`) and the instance does not use line chunking (`lineLength == 0`), nothing is appended. Otherwise the pending bytes (if any) are encoded as a final partial group: their bits are left-aligned into 5-bit characters and the last character is zero-padded on the right; then padding is applied as described below; `currentLinePos` is increased by the number of characters written by this call; finally, if the instance uses line chunking and `currentLinePos > 0` (the current line is not empty), the line separator is appended once.
   - 1 pending byte: 2 characters followed by 6 pad bytes; 2 pending bytes: 4 characters followed by 4 pad bytes; 3 pending bytes: 5 characters followed by 3 pad bytes; 4 pending bytes: 7 characters followed by 1 pad byte. Padding bytes are the instance's pad byte (default `=`) and are always written (for both alphabets), so a final group always has 8 output bytes.
4. The output buffer is created and grown on demand (see `ensureBufferSize` in the context); callers only look at `context.buffer[0 .. context.pos-1]`. Existing buffer content is preserved when it grows.

## 3. Input specification

- `in`: byte array (may be `null` for the end-of-input call).
- `inPos`, `inAvail`: start offset and number of bytes (`inAvail < 0` means end of input). `inAvail == 0` consumes nothing (but does not set `eof`).
- `context`: a `Context` whose state is carried over between calls; fresh contexts start with `modulus = 0`, `pos = 0`, `currentLinePos = 0`, `eof = false`, `buffer = null`.

## 4. Output specification

The context is updated in place: new output bytes are written to `context.buffer` starting at the previous `context.pos`; `pos`, `modulus`, the work area, `currentLinePos` and `eof` are updated. Example (standard alphabet, no chunking, one data call with the bytes of `"abc"` followed by an end-of-input call): `buffer[0..pos-1]` is the ASCII text `MFRGG===`. - Calls after `eof` is set are ignored (no output, no exception).
